sakka.notes: Sakka 03 is the Sakyan clan cross-reference. DPD has sakka 3 and sakkā 2 on taps such as sakkesu, but neither sense is in the packet. The English filter misses clan uses such as AN 10.46:1.1. DN 20:2.2 places the Buddha among the Sakyans and 14.10 names the god Purindada. Thag 21.1:57.1 likewise addresses the Buddha as sakka, then 58.4 compares him to thousand-eyed Sakka. Both need a choice finer than the whole sutta. The parallel Snp 2.12:4.1 spells the clan vocative sakya, which has its own dictionary lines. SN 10.2 calls its speaker a yakkha named Sakka and gives no royal title. MN 56:29.37 applies the divine epithets to the Buddha. MN 98:13.16 and Snp 3.9:68.4 apply Brahmā and Sakka to one accomplished in the three knowledges. SN 40.11 explicitly refers back to the Sakka discourse of SN 40.10 in its repetition instruction and chapter summary. In Snp 3.11:1.2 and Thig 7.1:7.1 the Pali tap includes sakka 2, but the English name falls a line later, so both deity mentions are missing. AN 7.66:13.6 gives Sunetta thirty-six births as Sakka where the entry gives thirty-five. The mapped AN 8.14–16 do not name the Sakyans. SN 2.3 is the Māgha/Vatrabhū reference, SN 10.2 the named yakkha, and SN 40.10 the visit to Moggallāna. Their neighboring page matches and the SN 9.7–9 citations do not establish appearances by the god.

sakuludāyī.notes: MN 77 and MN 79 place this wanderer at the peacocks’ feeding ground. AN 4.30 and AN 4.185 name him with Annabhāra and Varadhara. The mapped AN 4.28 and AN 4.29 contain neither meeting.

sakulā.notes: Thig 5.7 names Sakulā Therī and describes her clairvoyance. Its five verses are 97–101, while the entry starts at 98. AN 1.242 names the foremost nun in clairvoyance as bakulā in the local Pali and Sakulā in English. Tapping bakulā opens a separate lemma. AN 1.219–234 and AN 1.248–257 are adjacent lists. MN 90 identifies the sisters Somā and Sakulā by the greetings Pasenadi delivers. The text calls them sisters and leaves their marital status unstated. MN 89 is the neighboring Pasenadi discourse.

salalāgāra.notes: SN 52.8 locates Anuruddha in the salaḷāgāra at Sāvatthī. SN 52.7 gives only Sāvatthī. In DN 21:1.9.5 Sakka calls the hut salaḷāgārake, which opens the separate diminutive lemma salaḷāgāraka. DN 21:1.10.1 names the attendant Bhūjati, spelled Bhuñjatī in the entry.

sambara.notes: SN 11.10 names Sambara as the asura lord whom the seers curse. SN 11.23 has Vepacitti cite Sambara’s fate. Identifying the two lords with each other depends on the commentary. The mapped SN 11.9 and SN 11.24 do not name Sambara.

sambhūta.notes: DPD points to the four verses attributed to Sambhūta at Thag 4.7:4.5. The candidate identifies its elder by the name Sītavaniya and by Thag verse 6. Thag 1.6:1.5 explicitly credits Sītavaniya, who has his own DPD lemma, sītavaniya. The candidate belongs with that elder. Showing it as the biography of the poet at Thag 4.7 would conflate them. The chapter summary at Thag 4.12:5.4 also names Sambhūta among the four-verse poets.

samiddhi.notes: MN 133 gives the encounter after bathing at Tapodā and Thag 1.46 credits Samiddhitthero, a separate compound lemma. Sāriputta questions Samiddhi in AN 9.14. AN 9.13 is his exchange with Mahākoṭṭhita. SN 35.66–67 identify Samiddhi in compound titles. The mentions in AN 9.20 and SN 35.73 belong to chapter summaries.

samīti.notes: MN 5:31 identifies Samīti by his work on the chariot wheel while Paṇḍuputta watches. The Pali title is Anaṅgaṇasutta, printed as Aṅganasutta in the entry.

sanaṅkumāra.notes: SN 6.11 locates the Brahmā on the bank of the Sappinī and attributes the verse on lineage, knowledge and conduct to him. DN 3 quotes it under his name. DN 4, SN 6.10 and SN 6.12 are neighboring page matches. The Buddha himself recites the verse at SN 21.11:3.1–4. This explains the citation there. SN 21.10 and SN 21.12 do not give the verse.

sandhāna.notes: DN 25 names the Rājagaha householder who visits Nigrodha. The lay-disciple list names him at AN 6.120–139:1.14. AN 6.119 concerns Tapussa and AN 6.140 begins the series on greed.

santusita.notes: AN 8.36 names the godling who surpasses the other Tusita deities. SN 40.11 lists him by name. DN 11:75.1 uses the variant santussito, which opens santussita 1. The mapped AN 8.37 and SN 40.10 concern other subjects.

santuṭṭha.notes: DN 16 and SN 55.10 list Santuṭṭha separately from Tuṭṭha among the laymen who died at Ñātikā. Both describe his destiny as a non-returner and leave the particular heaven unnamed. The entry specifies Akaniṭṭha. SN 55.9 concerns disciples named Asoka or Asokā.

sappasoṇḍikapabbhāra.notes: DN 16 places the overhang in the Cool Grove at Rājagaha. The Upasena episode opens there at SN 35.69:1.1. SN 35.68 is Samiddhi’s question about the world.

sarabha.notes: The wanderer who recently left the training and kept silent when challenged appears in AN 3.64 in this corpus. The mapped AN 3.63 is at Venāgapura, and DPD’s AN 3.65 is at Kesamutta.

sarabhaṅga.notes: MN 116 lists Sarabhaṅga among the independently awakened Buddhas of Isigili. In Thag 7.5 the attributed elder describes breaking reeds for his hut and following Gotama’s training rules. The packet misses two uses in his verse. At 1.3 Sujato translates the name as Reed-breaker on the next line, and at 3.2 the English name falls a line earlier.

sarabhū.notes: SN 13.3 and SN 13.4 both name the Sarabhū among the five rivers. The adjacent SN 13.5 gives a simile about clay balls and the earth.
